title: UPPER and LOWER String Functions
description:
Some employee names and emails are stored with inconsistent casing. Write a query that returns `id`, the employee's `name` converted to **UPPER** case as `name_upper`, and the `email` converted to **LOWER** case as `email_lower`.

**Table: employees**

| Column | Type |
|--------|------|
| id | INT |
| name | VARCHAR |
| email | VARCHAR |
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT, name VARCHAR, email VARCHAR); INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1, 'Alice Johnson', 'ALICE@COMPANY.COM'), (2, 'Bob Smith', 'BOB@COMPANY.COM'), (3, 'carol davis', 'carol@company.com'), (4, 'DIANA PRINCE', 'DIANA@COMPANY.COM'), (5, 'evan brown', 'EVAN@COMPANY.COM');
solution_sql: SELECT id, UPPER(name) AS name_upper, LOWER(email) AS email_lower FROM employees

test_cases.description: Returns 5 rows with name in upper case and email in lower case

hints: `UPPER(column)` converts all characters to uppercase; `LOWER(column)` converts to lowercase.
Use the `AS` keyword to rename the result columns to `name_upper` and `email_lower`.
explanation: `UPPER(name)` transforms the name to all capitals regardless of its original casing, while `LOWER(email)` normalizes emails to all lowercase — useful for consistent storage or comparison.
